Model verification for Edinburgh: forecasts made 1/3/5/7 days ahead vs ERA5 reanalysis, last 40 days (temp_mae in °C, lower is better; wet_dry_hit_pct = share of days the model got right whether it would rain over 1 mm). 'Claude (this page)' is your own previous forecasts, scored the same way (its rain call counts a chance of 50% or more, or medium or high risk, as rain); use its biases to correct yourself. 'reliability' scores your own rain chances (Brier, 0 is perfect) against ECMWF ENS on the same days and against the window's wet-day share, and your weekly tilts for the extended-range weeks against ERA5's weekly mean. 'station' is the same check against EGPH's own observed daily highs and lows (METAR; complete the next day, so it includes the last week that ERA5 hasn't reached; half-hourly integer readings, so its highs run a few tenths low). station.tmin_by_night is the airport-trained correction of the models' lows by type of night (per lead: each model's all-night bias, and per class the nights, the mean model bias on such a night (bias) and the part the blend removes after shrinkage (used_bias)); recent_1day the last nights one day ahead; blend_by_night the blend's own logged lows scored at the airport by the type of night it forecast, out of sample

tmin_by_night.rule: type of night from the models' mean hourly total cloud and 10 m wind, 18:00-08:00 local: clear and calm = wind under 10 km/h and cloud under 30%; calm, broken cloud = wind under 10 km/h and cloud under 75%; otherwise cloudy or windy. Each model's all-night bias at the airport, plus the class's extra bias shrunk by n/(n+5) for n nights; ERA5 bias, unsplit, where a model has under 14 airport nights at a lead

items.title: ECMWF seasonal ensemble by month for Edinburgh vs ERA5 1991-2020 normals. This is Open-Meteo's default seasonal series: EC46 (run daily) for about the first 46 days, then SEAS5 (started on the 1st of each month), 51 members joined by member number, on a 36 km grid, so the first month or two are mostly EC46. Raw model output, not bias-corrected: the model's own climate at this point differs from ERA5's normal by month and lead (the SEAS5 winter call's model_climate.by_month gives bias_c, and pct_members_warmer_than_model_climate for SEAS5 alone against its own climate), so pct_members_warmer_than_normal here mixes the forecast with that bias. Compare the spread and the shares, not the absolute values

ECMWF's own implied calls on the cold-winter event, from the point members. pct_members_colder_than_normal (logged beside your call and scored as the rival 'ECMWF SEAS5') is the share of the 51 members of the default series above (EC46 for about 46 days, then SEAS5, joined by member number, so its December is mostly EC46) with a December-February mean of (daily max + min) / 2 below the ERA5 1991-2020 normal. It is raw model output, so it mixes the forecast with the model's own error at this point, and it is against ERA5, not the ERA5-Land the odds are scored on. pct_members_colder_than_model_climate is SEAS5 alone (model_climate.run_start is the first month of the reply; in the first days of a month the newest run can still be the month before): the share of its members whose December-February mean is below SEAS5's own climate for the same start month and lead (ECMWF's monthly anomaly, from its re-forecasts; model_climate.climate says which years). That removes the model's mean error at this point (model_climate.by_month gives it month by month as bias_c, the model climate minus the ERA5 normal) but not errors in the spread, and it is not calibrated on the model's past skill. model_climate.djf.pct_range_for_rounding is how far the 0.1 °C rounding of ECMWF's figures can move it; pct_same_members_colder_than_era5_normal is the same SEAS5 members against the ERA5 normal without the correction, so the three shares separate the EC46 part from the bias part. None of them is the answer: they are inputs to weigh

model_climate.note: The model climate is the mean of the past forecasts that SEAS5 makes for the same start month and the same lead. A share below this climate removes the mean error of the model at this point. It does not correct the spread of the members, the change in climate between the two periods, or the difference between ERA5 and ERA5-Land.

items.title: Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later; w1 and w2 are the parts of it carried by zonal wavenumbers 1 and 2: a pulse mostly in wave 1 tends to displace the vortex, one with a large wave-2 part to stretch and split it), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-11-14 are analysis.

items.title: Arctic Oscillation (AO), North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and Pacific-North American pattern (PNA) indices, NOAA CPC's standardised daily values (AO from 1000 hPa height, NAO and PNA from 500 hPa): last 10 days observed and CPC's GEFS forecast (31 members: mean/p10/p90/min/max, % negative). An index whose file failed this run is left out. Negative AO/NAO favours blocking and cold spells in the UK; positive, mild westerlies. A positive PNA goes with a deep Aleutian low, the pattern El Niño favours, which adds to the wave 1 that goes up into the stratosphere; a negative PNA during an El Niño means the atmosphere is not following it.

Slow climate drivers: QBO (monthly equatorial zonal wind at 30 and 50 hPa, m/s; easterly QBO makes a weak vortex and SSWs more likely), ENSO (weekly Niño 3.4 SST anomaly and the ONI and the Relative ONI, RONI, which takes the tropical mean warming out, °C; La Niña below -0.5, El Niño above +0.5; the El Niño tables call +1.0 to +1.5 strong and +1.5 or more very strong) and the MJO (last 10 days, Wheeler-Hendon phase 1-8 and amplitude; amplitude under 1 means weak). MJO phases 6-7 tend to favour a negative NAO 1-2 weeks later. More ENSO keys, each missing when its source failed (anomalies in °C against 1991-2020): regions_weekly, the last 8 weeks of CPC's four weekly Niño regions (1+2, 3, 3.4, 4) with e_index and c_index, the east and central Pacific indices; region_records, each region's latest week ranked among every week since September 1981 (rank 1 = the warmest, 'of' = weeks in the record), with the highest of the last 52 weeks and the previous record, the highest week before those 52; flavour, a word from E and C over the last 4 weeks by the rule given with it; same_weeks, those 4 weeks this year and the same weeks of the earlier years with the highest mean Niño 3.4 there (years_compared = years the record covers), each with its four regions, E, C and flavour, to show which past event this one is like; mei, PSL's Multivariate ENSO Index v2 (standardised, no unit: sea level pressure, SST, surface winds and outgoing longwave radiation over the tropical Pacific, so it measures the atmosphere's part too), the last 6 two-month seasons, and the latest ranked among the same season of every year since 1979, with previous_record the highest of the other years; relative_nino34, NOAA OISST v2.1 against PSL's 1991-2020 daily mean: the Niño 3.4 box (5°S-5°N, 170-120°W) anomaly minus the 20°S-20°N mean anomaly (sea cells every 1° of latitude and 2° of longitude; 'cells' = how many), as the mean of the last 'days' days (7, fewer in early January) and the latest day. relative_nino34 is NOT the RONI and will not match it: CPC's RONI also multiplies the difference by a variance factor, is a 3-month mean and comes from ERSST, while this is unscaled, about a week, and from OISST.

flavour.rule: E = Niño 1+2 - 0.5 x Niño 4 and C = 1.7 x Niño 4 - 0.1 x Niño 1+2 (the published approximation of Takahashi et al. 2011, from the weekly anomalies, °C). The larger of |E| and |C| says warm or cold; then east Pacific when E is more than twice C, central Pacific when C is more than twice E (both with the sign of a cold event turned over), mixed between; no word when neither reaches 0.5

periods.text: A changeable pattern is likely to continue, with areas of rain or showers affecting parts of the UK, particularly across the south and west. These will be interspersed with drier, colder interludes as shorter-lived ridges of high pressure develop. Weather patterns may become slower evolving during the latter stages of November, leading to some uncertainty over how much progress Atlantic frontal systems will make into the UK. Nonetheless, further rain or showers are likely at times, with the potential for some periods of strong winds. Incursions of milder air are likely towards the south, although it could remain on the cold side overall further north, where there is potential for overnight frosts and occasional wintry precipitation, particularly over higher ground.

The tracks of low pressure may shift farther south over the North Atlantic into December, as high pressure potentially builds between Scandinavia and Greenland. Whilst there remains some uncertainty over which of these features will have the greater influence on the weather in the UK, some rain is likely at times, particularly across southern areas, whilst northern and especially northwestern parts may become drier than normal. Milder incursions are possible in the south, although this pattern would also bring an increased chance of colder conditions developing, particularly in the north, along with associated winter hazards such as snow and ice.

sections.text: The Arctic Oscillation (AO) is currently negative as pressure/geopotential height anomalies across the Arctic are currently mostly positive and the AO is predicted to remain negative to neutral the next two weeks as pressure/geopotential height anomalies are predicted to remain mixed to positive the next two weeks. The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is currently negative with mostly positive pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland, and the NAO is predicted to remain negative to neutral the next two weeks as pressure/geopotential height anomalies are predicted to remain mixed to positive across Greenland the next two weeks. This week ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies are predicted to stretch from Greenland United Kingdom (UK) favoring troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Northern Europe with more ridging across Southern Europe. However next week as the ridging weakens across Greenland so will the troughing across Northern Europe. This pattern will favor normal to below normal temperatures across Northern Europe including the UK with normal to above normal temperatures across Southern Europe this week. However next week normal to above normal temperatures will become more widespread across much of Europe though some residual cold temperatures are possible across Scandinavia and the UK. The next two weeks predicted ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across the Beaufort Seas and the Central Arctic will favor troughing/ [...]

The widespread warmth across the Northern Hemisphere (NH) this past summer and now the fall has continued into November (see Figure). However, high-latitude blocking in the North Atlantic sector has resulted in colder temperatures in Europe and especially Siberia and into Northeast Asia (see Figure). Troughing in the Gulf of Alaska has resulted in very mild temperatures for North America (see Figure). However, the very large PV disruption ongoing, in my opinion will resolve into a stretched PV. Stretched PVs first result in cold temperatures in East Asia followed by a colder pattern in North America. So despite the indefinite reign of mild weather across North America predicted by the weather models, I expect colder temperatures to arrive ashore across North America late November and/or early December. And as I am fond of saying one good (PV) stretch deserves another. Figure. Estimate of the observed surface temperatures (°C; shading) from 01 Nov to 08 Nov 2026 based on GFS initializations and the GFS forecast from the 9 Nov 2026 run.

While the rest of the meteorological community has been focused on the super El Niño, my focus this fall has been stretched polar vortex (PV) events. Back in late September (28 Sep 2026) I noted a very early stretched PV and posed two questions to ponder. Could this be a foreshadowing by the atmosphere for the winter? Since 2013 the canonical sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) extended Greenland blocking pathway is no longer in operation, instead we seem to be in a paradigm where all PV disruptions of the cold kind are PV stretching (obviously an exaggeration but to first order true). Since then, I have been arguing with myself saying based on the SSW the best analog for November 2026 is November 2009. However, 2009 is clearly in the “before times,” and now there is a new Sherrif in town, or of you prefer a new paradigm in operation. In 2009 the SSW-negative NAO ruled and today we are under new management and the PV stretch-negative North Pacific Oscillation rules. And when the models first caught on to the possibility of an SSW and excitement was building for the expected tropospheric response of a long duration Greenland block/negative NAO, I shared with USA Today don’t be surprised if this all resolves as yet just another stretched PV (USA Today 26Oct2026). And I have juxtaposed and contrasted my thoughts with the almost universal expectation that super El Niño is simply too large and strong for the PV to have a meaningful impact on our weather. The super El Niño will defl [...]

This Week The AO is predicted to be negative this week (Figure 1) with mostly positive geopotential height anomalies currently across the Arctic and mixed geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitudes of the NH (Figure 2). With predicted i positive geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 2), the NAO is predicted to be negative this week as well. Figure 1. The predicted daily-mean AO at a) 10 hPa and at b) 1000 hPa from the 00Z 9 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. Gray lines indicate the AO index from each individual ensemble member, with the ensemble mean AO index given by the red line with squares. Ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies stretching from Greenland are predicted to support troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Northern Europe with ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Southern Europe this week (Figure 2). This pattern will support normal to below normal temperatures across Southern Europe with normal to below normal temperatures across Northern Europe including the UK this week (Figure 3). This week the general pattern across Asia is ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies centered across the Beaufort Sea forcing troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Northern and Western Asia with more ridging across Southern and Eastern Asia this week (Figure 2). This mostly zonal flow pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures across Asia with normal to below normal temperatures  [...]

Next Week With geopotential height anomalies becoming mostly mixed across the Arctic and with mixed geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitudes this period (Figure 5), the AO will likely remain close to neutral to slightly negative this period (Figure 1). With weak and mixed pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 5), the NAO will likely also trend towards neutral this period. Figure 5. Forecasted average 500 mb geopotential heights (dam; contours) and geopotential height anomalies (m; shading) across the Northern Hemisphere from 15 Nov to 19 Nov 2026. The forecasts are from the 00Z 9 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. Weak ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Greenland will continue to support troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Northern Europe with ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Southern Europe this period (Figure 5). However, the quasi-zonal flow pattern will support the spreading of normal to above normal temperatures across Europe with the best exception for normal to below normal temperatures in Scandinavia and the UK this period (Figure 6). Persistent albeit weakening ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies centered across the Beaufort Sea forcing troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Northern Asia with more ridging across Central and Southern Asia this period (Figure 5). This zonal flow pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures widespread acr [...]

Week Two With predicted mixed to positive geopotential height anomalies across the Arctic and mixed geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitudes this period (Figure 8), the AO will likely remain near neutral to slightly negative this period (Figure 1). With predicted weak but mostly positive pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 8), the NAO will likely also remain near neutral to slightly negative this period as well. Figure 8. Forecasted average 500 mb geopotential heights (dam; contours) and geopotential height anomalies (m; shading) across the Northern Hemisphere from 20 Nov to 24 Nov 2026. The forecasts are from the 00Z 9 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. Deepening troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitude North Atlantic will favor strengthening ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Europe this period (Figure 8). This pattern will favor widespread normal to below normal temperatures across much of Europe, though some residual cold temperatures are possible in Scandinavia and the UK this period (Figures 9). The pattern of troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Northern Asia with ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Southern Asia is predicted to persist this period (Figure 8). This pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures across most of Asia especially Central Asia with normal to below normal temperatures limited to Eastern Siberia this period (Figu [...]

30-day Today’s polar cap geopotential height anomalies (PCHs) plot currently shows cold/negative PCHs limited to the lower troposphere with warm/positive PCHs throughout the stratosphere and upper troposphere (Figure 11). However, this week, the warm/positive PCHs in the stratosphere are predicted to descend into the lower troposphere. This is followed by cold/negative PCHs in the upper stratosphere. Figure 11. Observed and predicted daily polar cap height (i.e., area-averaged geopotential heights poleward of 60°N) standardized anomalies. The forecast is from the 00Z 09 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. This week the predicted neutral PCHs in the lower troposphere (Figure 11) are consistent with the predicted negative to neutral surface AO (Figure 1). There can be a temporary strengthening of the negative AO over the weekend as the warm/positive PCHs descend to the surface. However, beginning next week when the reemergence of cold/negative PCHs in the lower troposphere (Figure 11) could push the surface AO to pop positive. Figure 12. Observed and predicted daily vertical component of the wave activity flux (WAFz) standardized anomalies, averaged poleward of 40-80°N. The forecast is from the 00Z 09 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. The large positive (upward) pulse of vertical Wave Activity Flux (WAFz) from the troposphere to the stratosphere or poleward heat transport in the stratosphere is starting in late October is winding down (Figure 12). But it does appear that it is sufficient to push the o [...]

Arctic Sea Ice I am and will continue to watch Arctic sea ice. Current conditions are shown in Figure 16. It has been shown that less sea ice in the North Atlantic sector of the Arctic weakens the polar vortex while less sea ice in the North Pacific sector strengthens the polar vortex. Sea ice has been growing a decent clip, but clearly more in the North Pacific sector than the North Atlantic sector and therefore Arctic sea ice anomalies continue to show a strong focus or weighting of negative anomalies towards the North Atlantic sector relative to the North Pacific sector and this is a robust signal of an overall weaker PV this winter. In fact with sea ice near normal in the North Pacific sector and well below normal in the North Atlantic sector looks nearly optimal for perturbing the PV. I believe that the lack of sea ice in the Barents-Kara Seas may have contributed to the record strong high-pressure Ural/Scandinavian blocking and the unprecedentedly early weak PV that so far resembles more of an SSW than the more common stretched PV this time of year. items.title: Analog winters for Edinburgh: the 5 past winters (since 1979/80) most like this autumn in vortex strength (mean 60°N 10 hPa wind over the last 30 days, m/s), ENSO (RONI (Niño 3.4 less the tropical mean), °C; now.distance_index says which, and oni is given beside it) and QBO (30 hPa wind, m/s), each in standard deviations of the record, with equal weight, closest first; for each, its major SSW date if any and Edinburgh's Dec/Jan/Feb mean temperature anomaly vs 1991-2020 (°C, ERA5) with snow and frost days. Five analogs are a small sample: treat them as a tilt in the odds, and compare with all_winters. chance_check says whether they say more than 10000 random sets of as many winters would (trend removed): within chance, they shouldn't move the odds. early_ssw_winters is every winter in the record with a major SSW by 31 December, the reference class when an early warming is under way or forecast, with the same check. enso_qbo_winters is a second reference set, the five nearest on ENSO and the QBO only, with its own chance_check: the vortex term can keep out a winter that matches on El Niño and the QBO. method_skill is how this method has done on the record: each past winter in turn matched against the others by today's rule and calendar window (leave one out), for the variables in use (in_use) and without the vortex term (without_vortex); djf_correlation is between the analogs' mean detrended Dec-Feb and the winter's own, against r_critical_5pct, the value chance reaches or passes about one time in 20 with as many winters (one-sided and approximate; a negative correlation is no result either way); djf_sign_right counts the winters whose sign (milder or colder than the trend) the analogs got right, against djf_sign_right_by_chance; ssw_brier scores the analogs' SSW share as a chance of a major SSW (0 is perfect) against ssw_base_rate_brier, always calling the other winters' rate. When verdict is no measurable skill, the analogs carry no information the record does not, and must not move the odds. novelty: today's distance to its nearest analog (nearest_now) against every past winter's distance to its own nearest (median, 90th percentile, largest), today's z-score on each variable, beyond_record for any variable outside the record's range, and outside_record when today is farther from its nearest analog than any past winter was: then no past winter is a true analog

Major sudden stratospheric warmings by the month they start, for the ssw_*_pct calls: the definition the calls are scored on, how often each month from November to February has had one since 1979/80 (reference_pct is the rate the calls are scored against), this season so far (NASA's analysis and GEOS-FP's 10-day forecast), and how dated calls made before each month began have scored (Brier, 0 is perfect): yours, and other people's public calls, which are here to be scored, not as evidence. el_nino_model, when present, scales the reference rates for this El Niño with an idealised model (rate_ratio is a range; its text, hindcast and live scores say how far to trust it; its input is the ONI, as the plan fixes, and sensitivity.roni, when present, gives the same figures with the RONI as the input, a sensitivity figure that is never logged or scored). after_ssw: how often another major SSW started within 30, 60 and 90 days of one, in the record since 1979 (all, and those by 31 December) and in the model. by_enso_qbo: how many winters since 1979/80 had a major SSW under the same definition (any: November to March; dec_feb; jan_feb) by El Niño class on the August-October ONI and on the RONI (very strong +1.5 or more, strong +1.0 to +1.5, weak to moderate +0.5 to +1.0, neutral, La Niña -0.5 or less; winters named with their SSW start dates when 8 or fewer), by the QBO's phase in October at 30 and at 50 hPa (west: wind 0 or more), and for this winter's cell (this_year: its class on the index the analogs use, and its QBO phase at 30 hPa), with each winter in the cell named. Each count comes with the share of all possible sets of as many winters from the record with as many or as few (random_sets_with_as_many_pct, random_sets_with_as_few_pct). A verdict of too few winters to tell means the group is so small that no count at all could fall outside chance (0 of 3 winters is one): it is not evidence of no difference, and it is not evidence of a difference. Within chance means a larger group that is no different from any winters. cells gives how many checks the table holds, how many fell outside chance, how many chance alone gives (expected_outside_by_chance, exact) and how many are too_few_to_tell. The groups at +1.0 or more hold a few winters each, so read them as counts. this_season.earliest_in_record: the earliest start in a season (from 1 July) of a major SSW in this record before this season, and whether this season's first one is earlier (this_is_earliest); call an event record-early only from this, and say the record is NASA MERRA-2 since its from_season

data.definition: a major sudden stratospheric warming starts in that month. On a day in the month, the zonal-mean wind at 60°N, 10 hPa (NASA MERRA-2, and GEOS-FP for this season) turns easterly. This occurs at least 20 westerly days after any earlier event. Before 30 April, the wind is westerly again for 10 days in a row (Charlton and Polvani). A reversal with no recovery is the final warming, and it does not count

el_nino_model.text: Five seasonal forecast systems from Copernicus give more major sudden stratospheric warmings in strong El Niño winters, 1.26 times the usual rate (1.17 to 1.36). Their tests cover the winters of 1993 to 2016 and show no sign that the effect grows faster as El Niño gets stronger. Thus the chance of a warming that starts in January goes from 22% to 27% (25% to 29%).

items.title: Central England Temperature (Met Office HadCET, monthly since 1659): the latest months against 1991-2020 with their rank, reference past winters (November to March, December-February against 1991-2020 and against their own era, ranks among all winters, coldest = 1) and how often a cold November has been followed by a cold December-February. Central England, not the location; pre-1979 'SSW' winters are inferred, not measured. enso_classes (null if Niño 3.4 could not be fetched): every winter since 1870/71 by El Niño class on the August-October mean of Niño 3.4 (HadISST) against its own era, classes fixed in advance (very strong +1.5 or more, strong +1.0 to +1.5, weak to moderate +0.5 to +1.0, neutral, La Niña -0.5 or less). Per class: the number of winters and, for November, December, January, February, March, December-February and late_minus_early (January-February minus November-December, so negative means the late winter was colder than the early winter), the mean in °C against each winter's own era (a 31-year mean, which takes out the long-term warming), colder (how many winters were below their era; for late_minus_early, how many had the colder late winter), and where the mean falls among 10,000 random sets of as many winters (random_5_95, random_sets_below_pct, verdict; within chance means any winters picked at random do as well). top_class_winters lists the very strong winters month by month. cells says how many class-by-month means were checked, how many fell outside chance and how many chance alone gives (about one in ten): one extreme cell among many is not proof. For the last 15 winters the 31-year window has only earlier years in it, so its mean is moved along the 61-year trend of the November-March mean (2015/16 and 2023/24, two of the very strong winters, are in that zone, and the move takes about 0.1 to 0.2 °C off them); Niño 3.4 for those years is against the earlier years only. this_year is this winter's class from CPC's ONI (RONI beside it), as the Niño 3.4 file lags. Central England, not the location, and a few winters per class

items.title: Global relative atmospheric angular momentum (the wind term of NASA's AAM, from the GEOS-FP analysis, no forecast), daily, in standard deviations from the MERRA-2 1991-2020 normal for the date, with the change over 7 days. High AAM is the El Niño state; its rise and fall (the tendency) is what the Global Wind Oscillation tracks. gwo: the GWO phase (1-8) and amplitude for the last 40 days, computed here from the same series

gwo.definition: Weickmann and Berry (2009): x = AAM tendency, y = AAM anomaly, both in sd; Wheeler-Hendon octants, anticlockwise; two days behind the AAM analysis

items.title: Mountain torque by region (global, East Asia/Tibet, the Rockies, the Andes), drawn by this page from the GFS analyses: standard deviations from the 1991-2020 normal, the GFS forecast to day 7 thin after the bar, and the global AAM tendency below. Positive = higher pressure on the east side of the mountains, the atmosphere gaining westerly momentum

Mountain torque by region, computed by this page from the 1° GFS surface pressure and orography (four analyses a day, and the 00Z run to day 7): global, East Asia (15-60°N, 70-150°E, the Tibetan Plateau), North America (the Rockies) and South America (the Andes), in hadleys (1e18 N m, on the reanalysis's scale) and in sd from the NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 normal for 1991-2020. Positive = higher surface pressure east of the mountains than west (in East Asia, a cold surge's high pressed against the plateau), which gives the atmosphere westerly momentum; with friction it drives the global AAM tendency (aam_tendency, NASA, two days behind). summary: the latest day, 7-day means, the largest day of the last two weeks per region, the forecast's extremes

items.title: ECMWF extended range (EC46) to day 46, drawn by this page: each member's Arctic (60-90°N) mean sea-level pressure and NAO (Azores minus Iceland) in standard deviations against NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 for 1991-2020, the ensemble mean thick. A rise in the Arctic panel is high pressure over the pole (a negative AO); a fall in the NAO panel is a blocked, negative NAO. The line at day 15 is where the medium range ends

ECMWF extended range (EC46, 51 members via Open-Meteo) to day 46, at the surface: the Arctic index is the cos-weighted 60-90°N mean sea-level pressure (positive = high pressure over the pole = a negative-AO pattern, the surface end of a stratospheric event coupling down), the NAO the Azores-minus-Iceland pressure (negative = blocked NAO-), both in sd against NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 for 1991-2020 after the model's own offset is taken off. days: ensemble mean, 10th/90th percentiles and the share of members at +1 sd or more (Arctic) or -1 or below (NAO) each day; weeks: Monday-Sunday means; headline: the peak, the low and the days past day 15; model_climate: the weekly ensemble-mean anomalies in hPa against ECMWF's re-forecast climate (all 100 members), which need no reanalysis. Extended-range skill for the AO and NAO is modest past week 3: read shifts in the mean and the share of members, not a single date

Winter base rates for Edinburgh (since 1950/51; ERA5-Land at the point for the cold winter and the cold spell, ERA5's 0.25° cell for the wet winter and the stormy winter): how often each of the four winter-outlook events happened, under the exact definitions the odds use, for 1991-2020, the last 15 winters and all of them; the lines the wet and stormy winters are judged against (djf_precip_normal_mm, storm_days_normal: the 1991-2020 means); the last 15 winters one by one (with djf_precip_vs_normal_pct and storm_days); this season so far (precipitation as a percentage of normal for the December-February days in, and the stormy days so far: the stormy winter has happened once storm_days_so_far is above storm_days_normal); and how your own past calls scored (Brier score, 0 is perfect, against always calling the 1991-2020 base rate; null until a winter is over). The ERA5 gust is for a whole grid cell, so a station's gust is often stronger. by_el_nino (null if neither index could be fetched): the same winters by El Niño class on the August-October value, once on CPC's ONI and once on the RONI (Niño 3.4 less the tropical mean, so a warmer ocean does not read as El Niño), classes fixed in advance (very strong +1.5 or more, strong +1.0 to +1.5, weak to moderate +0.5 to +1.0, neutral, La Niña -0.5 or less); this_year gives this winter's class on each. Per class: the winters (named when 8 or fewer); counts of cold_winter, cold_spell, wet_winter and stormy_winter under the exact definitions above, each with the share of all possible sets of as many winters from the record with as many or as few (verdict within chance means the class is no different from any winters; too few winters to tell means the class is so small that no count could fall outside chance, which is not evidence either way); and the December-February, December, January and February means in °C with the record's linear warming trend taken out (trend_c_per_decade), with how many were colder than the trend and where each mean falls among 10,000 random sets of as many winters. strongest lists every winter at +1.0 or more one by one. since_1990_at_1_0_or_more is the same for the winters since 1990/91 at +1.0 or more, checked against the other winters since 1990/91 only: the fixed 1991-2020 cold-winter line is easier to miss now that winters are milder. cells says how many checks a table holds, how many fell outside chance, how many chance alone gives (expected_outside_by_chance) and how many are too_few_to_tell. The classes at +1.0 or more hold only a handful of winters each, so read them as tilts, not as rules

definitions.cold_winter: December to February as a whole is colder than its 1991-2020 normal at the location (ERA5-Land daily mean temperature)
definitions.cold_spell: at least one run of 5 or more days in a row from 1 November to 31 March. Each day of the run has a minimum of -3 °C or lower, or at least 5 cm of lying snow at the location (ERA5-Land)
definitions.wet_winter: December to February as a whole has more precipitation than its 1991-2020 mean at the location (ERA5, 0.25° grid)
definitions.stormy_winter: December to February has more stormy days than its 1991-2020 mean at the location. A stormy day has a gust of 70 km/h or more (ERA5 daily highest 10 m gust, 0.25° grid)
definitions.gust_note: ERA5 gives one gust for a whole grid cell. A gust at a station is often stronger, mostly on high or open ground.

analysis.headline: Rain on Sunday 15 November brings ice on Monday morning. A wetter front on Tuesday 17 November starts as snow on the Pentlands. An easterly with showers follows on 19 November.
analysis.summary:
No Met Office warnings are in force for Edinburgh. At 18:20 UTC the airport had 9 °C, light rain, a south-west wind of 37 km/h and 1002 hPa.

A cold front brings rain on Sunday 15 November. Frost and ice follow on Monday morning. A second, wetter front on Tuesday 17 November meets cold air, so it starts as sleet or snow on the hills. On 19 November a deep low sits south of Scotland and gives a cold easterly with showers. A ridge brings frost on 20-21 November.

The 10 hPa vortex wind is westerly again after the major SSW of 10-12 November. About half of the ECMWF members bring a high polar cap down to 500 hPa on 24-28 November. The models put the high over Scandinavia and the low to the west, so Edinburgh stays near normal in that week.

days.summary:
Observed: the airport fell to 2 °C in the early hours and reached 10 °C at 12:20-13:50 UTC. At 18:20 UTC it had 9 °C, a dew point of 5 °C and light rain from broken cloud at 4200 ft.

The rain is very light. Every ensemble gives 0% of members above 1 mm, except GEM ENS with 10%. The hourly guidance has 0.0 mm to midnight.

The south-west wind increases this evening. The METAR already has a mean wind of 37 km/h, more than the 18-21 km/h in the hourly guidance. The hourly gusts reach 47-55 km/h at 21:00-23:00.
days.wind: SW, 20-37 km/h, gusts 45-55 km/h at 21:00-23:00 (GEM 71 km/h, ARPEGE 64 km/h, GFS 56 km/h)

days.summary:
Drizzle starts near 03:00. The cold front brings the main rain at 11:00-16:00, with 1.3-1.5 mm an hour at 12:00-13:00. Showers end near 20:00.

Chance above 1 mm: 100% in ECMWF ENS, GEFS, AIFS ENS, GEM ENS and AIGEFS, 88% in ICON-EPS and 78% in UKMO ENS. Ensemble means are 4.4-11.4 mm. Single runs give 2.5 mm (ARPEGE) to 11.3 mm (GEM). The hourly sum is about 7 mm and the blend has 6.3 mm, so I expect 4-9 mm.

The temperature falls from 8.8 °C at 10:00 to 4.7 °C at 16:00. The freezing level falls from 1510 m at 10:00 to 800 m at 15:00 and 610 m at 23:00. The 850 hPa means reach -4.7 °C (ECMWF ENS) and -5.6 °C (GEFS) at 18 UTC.

So it is rain in the city. The Pentlands tops get sleet or wet snow late in the afternoon. GEFS has snow at the end of the rain in 68% of members, AIFS ENS in 2% and ECMWF ENS in 0%.

The roads stay wet as the air cools. ECMWF ENS gives ice in 88% of members and GEFS in 71%, but AIFS ENS and AIGEFS give 29%. The models split on the low: ECMWF HRES -0.4 °C, GEM 0.0 °C, UKMO 3.8 °C. The blend gives the airport 0.8 °C, so I set 1 °C near midnight.
days.wind: SW, 20-25 km/h, gusts 40-50 km/h to 06:00 (GEM 68 km/h, ARPEGE 66 km/h), light near 10:00, then W to NW 15-17 km/h, gusts 31-41 km/h after the front

days.summary:
The cold air clears the cloud after 03:00. The hourly guidance has 0.2 °C at 07:00, with a feels-like temperature near -4.5 °C. Wet paths and roads can freeze.

Lows: ECMWF ENS mean -1.6 °C (frost in 100% of members), GEFS -1.4 °C (97%), ECMWF HRES -2.0 °C and GEM -1.7 °C. UKMO, ICON and GFS give 0.2-0.7 °C. The blend gives the airport -1.4 °C, with frost at 70%.

The blend calls the night cloudy or windy, with 48% cloud and 10.5 km/h of wind. That is just above the calm limit, and the hourly sky is clear from 04:00. Nights like this ran cold at the airport, so I set -1.5 °C. Rural hollows can fall to -3 °C.

A cold north-westerly gives a dry, bright day. Chance above 1 mm: AIFS ENS 24%, ECMWF ENS and AIGEFS 10%, ICON-EPS 8%, UKMO ENS 6%, GEFS 3% and GEM ENS 0%. An early shower on the hills can be sleet or snow, with snow in 16% of AIFS ENS and 6% of ECMWF ENS members.

Highs: UKMO ENS 4.7 °C, blend 4.4 °C, ICON-EPS 4.2 °C, ECMWF ENS 3.7 °C and GEFS 2.9 °C. My highs ran 0.5 °C cold, so I set 4.5 °C. The wind falls calm after 15:00 and the temperature is 2 °C by 17:00, so frost forms again in the evening.
days.wind: W to NW, 12-15 km/h, gusts 25-31 km/h, calm after 15:00 (ECMWF HRES gusts 49 km/h, GFS 42 km/h)

days.summary:
Cloud and rain arrive near dawn. ECMWF ENS 6-hour means are 2.7, 4.4 and 3.0 mm at 06-12, 12-18 and 18-24 UTC.

Chance above 1 mm: AIFS ENS and GEM ENS 100%, ICON-EPS 98%, GEFS and AIGEFS 97%, ECMWF ENS 90% and UKMO ENS 89%. Ensemble means are 11.2-20.4 mm, and the ECMWF ENS 90th percentile is 22.6 mm. The blend has 13.7 mm. GFS has 26.9 mm and GEM 56.1 mm, both far above the other runs.

The front meets cold air. At 06 UTC the 850 hPa means are -2.5 °C (ECMWF ENS), -2.4 °C (GEFS) and -3.2 °C (GEM ENS), and the GEFS 10th percentile is -5.1 °C. AIFS ENS is milder, at -0.4 °C. So the rain starts as snow on the Pentlands and as sleet or rain in the city, then turns to rain.

Snow members: AIFS ENS 78%, GEFS 77% and GEM ENS 14%. ECMWF ENS has lying snow in 10% and ice in 39%. ICON-EPS gives a snow risk of 5-15% at 00-06 UTC, and GFS has 0.56 cm of snow.

Lows: blend 0.8 °C at the airport (frost 29%) and ECMWF ENS mean 1.0 °C, early in the night. I set 0.5 °C. Highs: blend 6.1 °C with a spread of 3.5 °C, ECMWF ENS 4.6 °C, GEFS 4.7 °C and AIFS ENS 7.1 °C. I set 6 °C.
days.wind: Southerly, 15-25 km/h, gusts 45-55 km/h (GFS 68 km/h, ARPEGE 62 km/h, GEM 54 km/h, ECMWF HRES 54 km/h)

days.summary:
The low moves slowly near the UK, so showery rain continues. Chance above 1 mm: AIFS ENS 90%, AIGEFS 87%, GEM ENS 71%, ICON-EPS 70%, GEFS 68%, UKMO ENS 67% and ECMWF ENS 61%. My medium days rained on 63% of days, and most shares sit above that, so I set 70%.

Amounts differ. UKMO has 15.4 mm and GFS 6.1 mm, but ECMWF HRES has 1.2 mm and GEM 0.4 mm. The blend has 3.9 mm.

The 850 hPa means are -1 to -2 °C in ECMWF ENS, GEFS and GEM ENS. So it is rain in the city and wet snow only on the higher tops. ECMWF ENS has lying snow in 6% of members and GEFS has snow in 10%.

Lows: blend 3.0 °C and ECMWF ENS 2.2 °C. I set 2.5 °C. Highs: blend 7.8 °C with a spread of 2.4 °C, ECMWF ENS 5.7 °C and AIFS ENS 7.4 °C. I set 7 °C.
days.wind: Light and variable, 5-15 km/h, gusts 25-35 km/h (ICON 51 km/h, ECMWF HRES 37 km/h)

days.summary:
Most models now put a deep low south of Scotland. ECMWF HRES has 978 hPa over southern England at 13:00. ICON-EU has 980 hPa over Ireland and NAVGEM 980 hPa over the Low Countries. GEM keeps 982 hPa west of Ireland.

So Edinburgh gets an easterly or north-easterly from the North Sea. UKMO has -2 to -4 °C at 850 hPa over Scotland. The North Sea is 0.77 °C above its 1991-2020 normal, so showers are rain near sea level and sleet on the hills.

Chance above 1 mm: GEM ENS 71%, AIFS ENS 51%, GEFS and AIGEFS 35%, ECMWF ENS 33%, ICON-EPS 28% and UKMO ENS 0%. ICON has 18.2 mm and gusts of 67 km/h, an outlier. I set 35%.

Lows: blend 1.7 °C (frost 18%), ECMWF ENS 0.8 °C and GEFS 0.3 °C. I set 1 °C. Highs: blend 7.3 °C, ECMWF ENS 5.6 °C, GEFS 4.7 °C and UKMO 4.8 °C. I set 6 °C.
days.wind: E to NE, 15-25 km/h, gusts 35-50 km/h (ICON 67 km/h, ECMWF HRES 50 km/h, UKMO 22 km/h)

days.summary:
A ridge brings a mostly dry, cold day. Chance above 1 mm: GEM ENS 19%, ICON-EPS, GEFS, ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS and AIGEFS 10%, and UKMO ENS 6%. I set 10%.

The blend now calls the night cloudy or windy, with 47% cloud and 11.2 km/h of wind. It gives the airport -0.2 °C, with frost at 45%. Frost in members: GEFS 71%, ECMWF ENS 63%, AIFS ENS 57%, AIGEFS 29%, UKMO ENS 28% and GEM ENS 0%. If the wind drops under 10 km/h, the airport will fall to -2 °C or lower. I set -0.5 °C.

Highs differ: UKMO 0.7 °C, GEFS 4.0 °C, ECMWF ENS 5.5 °C and GEM 7.9 °C, so the blend spread is 6.9 °C. I set 5.5 °C. Fog can form in the morning.
days.wind: N to NE, 5-15 km/h, gusts 15-35 km/h (GEM 43 km/h, ICON 43 km/h)

medium_range.summary:
I weight the ensembles over the single runs from day 5. Confidence is low after 20 November.

21-22 November: a ridge, then the next Atlantic front.
- ECMWF HRES has 1015-1020 hPa over the UK at 13:00 on 21 November. AIFS (machine learning) and GEM have 1020-1022 hPa, and JMA has a 1025 hPa high over the UK.
- The blend calls the night of 20-21 November calm with broken cloud. It gives the airport -0.7 °C, with frost at 52%, and its correction rests on 10 nights of that class.
- Rain returns late on 21 November and on 22 November. ECMWF ENS gives 61% and 71% of members above 1 mm, GEFS 29% and 32%, GEM ENS 62% on both days.
- GFS has 29.6 mm on 22 November and 24.8 mm on 23 November, an outlier. Most runs give 0-5 mm.

23-30 November: high pressure to the north and north-east, lows to the west.
- The ECMWF ENS mean on 24 November has a 995 hPa low south of Greenland and 1015-1020 hPa over Scandinavia. The GEFS mean has a 1000 hPa low over Ireland.
- JMA has a 1040-1060 hPa high from Greenland to Iceland, 1035 hPa over Norway and a 1000-1005 hPa low south-west of Ireland. That gives the UK an easterly.
- ECMWF HRES has a 996 hPa low over Northern Ireland and south-west Scotland on 24 November. AIFS and GEM have a broad trough near 1002-1006 hPa.
- On 29 November AIFS has a low near 975 hPa south of Iceland and a 1035 hPa high over Scandinavia, so a southerly. The GEFS mean has 1025 hPa over Greenland and 1000 hPa south of Iceland.
- The AIFS ENS spread is 12-18 hPa near Iceland on 24 November and 18-25 hPa from Iceland to the UK on 29 November.

Temperatures and rain, 23-28 November:
- ECMWF ENS mean highs are 6.7-8.3 °C and mean lows 3.0-4.1 °C, near normal. GEFS is colder, with mean highs of 5.9-7.2 °C.
- Chance above 1 mm: ECMWF ENS 67-75%, GEFS 35-68%, AIFS ENS 51-78% and GEM ENS 33-67%.
- The GEFS 850 hPa mean is -0.7 to -2.5 °C, with a 10th percentile of -5 to -7 °C. The AIFS ENS mean is -1.4 to +0.6 °C and the GEM ENS mean -0.8 to +1.9 °C.

What ties it together: the troposphere answers the major SSW in the last week of November. A block forms to the north and north-east. The air upwind is only moderately cold, so Edinburgh gets a raw south-easterly with rain at times. Snow falls mostly on the hills.

What can make this wrong: the block can sit further west, near Iceland, as JMA shows. Then a north-easterly brings colder air. GEFS keeps a cold tail, with snowfall in 6-10% of members on 25-28 November.
signals: Ice and frost: ECMWF ENS gives ice in 88% of members on 15 November and frost in 100% on 16 November. The blend gives the airport -1.4 °C on 16 November (frost 70%) and -0.7 °C on 21 November (frost 52%).

Snow: on 17 November AIFS ENS has snowfall in 78% of members and GEFS in 77%. ECMWF ENS has lying snow in 10%. On 15 November the freezing level falls to 610-800 m, so sleet or wet snow reaches the Pentlands tops.
Rain: ensemble means are 4.4-11.4 mm on 15 November and 11.2-20.4 mm on 17 November. GEM has 56.1 mm and GFS 26.9 mm on 17 November, both outliers.

Easterly: on 19 November ECMWF HRES, ICON-EU, NAVGEM and JMA put a 978-985 hPa low south of Scotland. UKMO has -2 to -4 °C at 850 hPa, so North Sea showers are rain at the coast and sleet on the hills.

AO and NAO (NOAA CPC): the observed AO is -0.87 and the NAO -1.36 on 14 November. GEFS takes the AO to +1.01 on 17 November, then to -1.48 on 29 November (90% of members negative). The NAO is near 0 to 27 November, then -0.46 on 29 November (74% negative).
PNA: +1.60 observed. GEFS keeps it at +0.40 to +1.50, with 0% of members negative. So the atmosphere follows El Niño, and the deep Aleutian low adds to wave 1.
ECMWF regimes (13 November): NAO- at 88-97% on 17-18 November. Blocking leads on 22-28 November at 34-54% and again on 5-12 December at 31-37%.
EPO: GEFS reaches -0.98 on 18 November and has 48% of members at -1 or below on 21 November. ECMWF ENS reaches -0.72 on 24 November (35% on 25 November), and AIFS ENS -0.60 on 19 November.

AAM and GWO: AAM is +2.91 sd on 14 November, with a 7-day change of +2.61. The GWO is in phase 6 at amplitude 3.08 on 12 November, the high-AAM, El Niño-like state. The East Asian torque of +4.03 sd on 8 November drove it, and the GFS has no new torque event to 21 November (peak +0.57 sd).

Heat flux (60°N ring, 100 hPa): a second pulse on 21-23 November, with ECMWF HRES 31.0, AIFS 32.1, GEM 29.3 and GFS 27.1 K m/s. The severe-weather.eu ensemble means (45-75°N) peak near 20-21 K m/s, under their 90th percentile of 26.2 K m/s.

Upwind cold (ECMWF ENS, 850 hPa): on 24-28 November, 24-31% of members reach -8 °C over Oslo and 22-29% reach it over Stockholm. Over Helsinki, 31-39% reach it, but only 6-12% reach it over Copenhagen. Oslo has snow cover in 71-76% of members, Stockholm and Copenhagen in 0-2%.
Snow cover: Eurasia has 14.55 million km², below the normal of 16.06 million km² and rank 41 of 61. The source region for an easterly is not snow-covered yet.

Sea temperatures (OISST against 1991-2020): the North Sea is +0.77 °C, with 36% of cells above +1 °C, so coast snow is marginal. The tripole is -0.61, the positive-NAO pattern. The open Barents and Kara Seas are +1.73 °C.

MJO: the analysed OMI is phase 4 at amplitude 1.08 on 10 November, now active. ECMWF ENS and the bias-corrected GEFS hold phase 4 near 1.2-1.5 to about 16 November, then go inside the circle. Neither reaches phases 6-7.

model_agreement.summary:
To 16 November the models agree well. A windy, dry evening comes first, then rain on Sunday in every run, then a cold, mostly dry Monday. They differ on the amount on 15 November (2.5-11.3 mm) and on the low on Monday morning (-2.0 to +0.7 °C).

On 17 November every ensemble is wet (89-100% above 1 mm). Most single runs give 9.6-18.5 mm, but GFS has 26.9 mm and GEM 56.1 mm. On 19 November most physics runs now put the low south of Scotland, and GEM keeps it west of Ireland. On 20 November the highs split from 0.7 °C (UKMO) to 7.9 °C (GEM).

From 23 November the physics runs keep lows near or west of the UK. AIFS (machine learning) puts a southerly ahead of a deep low on 29 November. JMA alone has a strong Greenland-Iceland high and an easterly on 24 November.

On the 40-day scorecard against ERA5, ICON is best one day ahead (0.6 °C), then the blend (0.7 °C) and AIFS (0.9 °C). ECMWF HRES and AIGFS run 1.1-1.6 °C cold on highs. At the airport every model runs warm on lows, by 0.4 °C (GEM) to 2.7 °C (GFS) one day ahead. My own lows ran 1.4 °C warm there and my highs 0.5-1.0 °C cold, and I correct for both.

models.view: 3.9 mm and a low of -0.4 °C on 15 November. Dry and cold on 16 November (-2.0 °C, 3.5 °C). 11.7 mm and gusts of 54 km/h on 17 November. A 978 hPa low over southern England on 19 November, a ridge on 21 November and a 996 hPa low near Northern Ireland on 24 November. Its highs run 1.3 °C cold on the scorecard.

100% above 1 mm on 15 November (mean 5.9 mm) and 90% on 17 November (mean 12.3 mm, lying snow in 10%). Frost in 100% of members on 16 November and 63% on 20 November. Rain in 67-75% of members on 23-27 November, with mean highs of 6.7-8.3 °C.

AIFS has 8.8 mm on 15 November and 12.6 mm on 17 November. It is milder on 17-18 November (lows 3.0-5.1 °C). It has a 1022 hPa ridge on 21 November and a 975 hPa low south of Iceland on 29 November. AIFS ENS has the most snow members on 17 November (78%) and the wettest 18 November (90%).

GFS is the wettest physics run on 17 November (26.9 mm, 0.56 cm of snow, gusts 68 km/h) and on 22-23 November (29.6 and 24.8 mm). GEFS is the coldest ensemble: an 850 hPa mean of -6.7 °C on 16 November and a 10th percentile near -7 °C on 27-28 November. GEFS also rebuilds the 10 hPa vortex fastest.

AIGFS has 7.0 mm on 15 November and 18.5 mm on 17 November. It is mild and dry on 21-23 November. AIGEFS gives 97% above 1 mm on 17 November and 87% on 18 November, and the highest mean on 15 November (11.4 mm).

ICON has the best one-day score (0.6 °C) and the top weight in the blend to 16 November. It has 4.6 mm on 15 November and 9.6 mm on 17 November. On 19 November it has 18.2 mm and gusts of 67 km/h, an outlier. ICON-EPS gives a snow risk of 5-15% early on 17 November.

UKMO has 6.9 mm on 15 November, 12.8 mm on 17 November and 15.4 mm on 18 November. It is the coldest run on 20 November, with a high of 0.7 °C. UKMO ENS gives 0% above 1 mm on 19 November and frost in 67% of members on 16 November.

GEM has gusts of 68-71 km/h on 14-15 November and 56.1 mm on 17 November, a large outlier. It keeps the 19 November low west of Ireland and is mild on 19-23 November (lows 5.0-7.5 °C). GEM ENS is the mildest ensemble after 21 November.

ARPEGE has 2.5 mm and gusts of 66 km/h on 15 November and 14.6 mm on 17 November. JMA has a 985 hPa low over England on 19 November and a 1025 hPa ridge on 21 November. It has a 1040-1060 hPa high from Greenland to Iceland on 24 November, the most blocked run. NAVGEM has a 980 hPa low over the Low Countries on 19 November and a ridge on 21 November.

extended_range.summary:
The ECMWF weekly maps, regimes, meteogram, Hovmöller, MJO and 46-day wind charts are from the 13 November run. The EC46 surface indices are from the 14 November run, and Simon Lee's index is from the 12 November run.

Edinburgh weekly meteogram (medians as I read them):
- 2 m temperature: about -2.7 °C for the week to 23 November, then about +0.5 °C for the week to 30 November. It is +0.3 to +0.7 °C in the weeks to 7, 14, 21 and 28 December.
- Precipitation: about 5 mm below normal to 23 November, then about +8 mm to 30 November and near normal after that.
- Pressure: below the model climate to 30 November, then near normal.

Weekly maps:
- 23-30 November: 500 hPa heights high over Scandinavia and 10-14 dam low west of Ireland. MSLP is +10 to +20 hPa over northern Scandinavia and -5 to -10 hPa over Ireland. Scotland is 0 to +1 °C in a south-easterly.
- 7-14 December: high pressure over Greenland, Iceland and Scandinavia, low pressure over the south-west Atlantic. The UK sits between them at 0 to +1 °C.
- 21-28 December: high 500 hPa heights over Greenland and the UK, low heights over the Baltic. That gives a north-westerly on the east side of a ridge, with the UK at 0 to +1 °C.

EC46 500 hPa over the North Pole: heights stay above normal over Greenland and the Canadian Arctic in all four weeks to 21 December. That is a negative AO, and it weakens in the week from 14 December.

EC46 surface indices (51 members):
- Arctic index: -1.19 sd on 17 November, then a peak of +0.76 sd on 26 November, with 45% of members above +1 sd. Weekly means are +0.64 and +0.59 sd for the weeks from 23 and 30 November (34-36% above +1 sd), then +0.21, -0.14 and -0.15 sd.
- NAO: -0.01, -0.35 and -0.22 sd in the weeks from 23 November, 30 November and 7 December, with 16-22% of members below -1 sd. Against the model climate it is 5.5-7.9 hPa below normal from 30 November to 27 December.
- Skill for the AO and NAO is modest past week 3, so I read the shifts and shares, not single dates.

Hovmöller (35-60°N):
- At 0°, a trough sits near the UK on about 17-20 November and a ridge on about 21-25 November.
- At 25-50°E a ridge covers about 14-22 November. After that the anomalies are weak, 2-4 dam against a spread of 6-12 dam.
- I see no window with a trough at 25-50°E and a ridge to the west. So the chart shows no northerly spell for Edinburgh.

MJO: ECMWF ENS (RMM) goes from phase 2-3 near 1.8 to phase 4 near 1.5 by day 5. It is near 1 by day 10 and inside the circle by day 15. The bias-corrected GEFS holds phase 4 near 1.2 to 16 November, then stays inside the circle to 28 November. Neither reaches phases 6-7, so the MJO gives no push to a negative NAO.

Met Office (19 November to 13 December): changeable to 28 November, with colder interludes, frost and wintry falls on high ground in the north. Then high pressure between Scandinavia and Greenland, lows further south and a drier north with a colder chance.
- I agree on the pattern and on a drier north in early December.
- I differ on temperature. The ECMWF weekly maps keep Scotland at 0 to +1 °C, because the air upwind is not very cold. So I call those weeks near normal.

AER (Judah Cohen, 9 November, 5 days old): the AO negative to neutral for two weeks and a stretched vortex. I agree on the stretch and on a short positive AO, which GEFS has at +0.5 to +1.0 on 16-22 November. I differ on late November, because GEFS takes the AO to -1.48 on 29 November.

weeks.pattern: Blocking leads at 34-54% on 22-28 November. A Scandinavian high and a trough west of Ireland give a south-easterly with rain at times. The meteogram median is about +0.5 °C.
No regime leads: Blocking 28-36%, NAO+ 19-35% and NAO- 9-27%. The EC46 Arctic index stays near +0.6 sd and the NAO near -0.35 sd. A mixed flow, often from the south.
Blocking leads at 31-37% on 7-12 December. High pressure over Greenland and Scandinavia, lows over the south-west Atlantic. The UK sits between them at 0 to +1 °C.

NAO+ 23-30% and Blocking 16-30%, so no regime leads clearly. The 10 hPa vortex is near 40 m/s in the 46-day chart, which favours westerlies. The EC46 Arctic index is -0.14 sd and the UK is 0 to +1 °C.
High 500 hPa heights over Greenland and the UK, low heights over the Baltic. That gives a north-westerly on the east side of a ridge. The UK is 0 to +1 °C.

extended_range.regimes:
ECMWF regime probabilities (13 November run):
- Atlantic Ridge 100% on 13-14 November and NAO+ 100% on 15 November.
- NAO- 97% on 17 November and 88% on 18 November, then 39-40% on 19-20 November.
- Blocking is the most likely regime on 22-28 November, at 54% on 22 and 24 November and 34% on 28 November.
- On 29 November to 4 December no regime leads: Blocking 28-33%, NAO+ 19-33% and NAO- 15-27%.
- Blocking leads again on 5-12 December at 31-37%, with NAO+ at 22-35%.
- From 13 December NAO+ is 23-30% and Blocking 16-30%, so no regime leads clearly.

Simon Lee's index (12 November run) uses a different scheme, so I compare only the time of the shifts. NAO+ peaks near +1.1 sd on 18-19 November. Scandinavian Blocking peaks near +0.6 sd on 22-23 November. NAO- rises to about +0.8 sd from 1 to 19 December.

The two schemes agree on a block from about 22 November and on a lean to NAO- or Blocking in early December. They disagree on 17-18 November: ECMWF has NAO-, but Lee's older run has NAO+.

For Edinburgh, a Scandinavian high with lows to the west gives a south-easterly. That brings rain on the edge of fronts and frost on clear nights. North Sea showers in an easterly are rain near sea level and sleet or snow on the hills. Snow at the coast needs much colder Baltic air than the runs show now.

stratosphere.summary:
Strength now:
- The 60°N wind at 10 hPa was easterly on 10-12 November. NASA GEOS had -2.9 m/s on 11 November and -2.1 m/s on 12 November, a record low for the date.
- On NASA MERRA-2 since 1979/80, this SSW (start 10 November) is the earliest in the record, before the 4 December 1981 event.
- Today it is westerly again. Single runs give 3.3-3.8 m/s, the ECMWF ENS mean 4.0 m/s, GEPS 3.6 m/s and the GEFS 06Z mean 3.1 m/s. The severe-weather.eu 00Z analysis has 2.7 m/s.
- NASA's climatology for 14 November has a record low of 10.0 m/s, a 10th percentile of 20.1 m/s and a mean of 29.7 m/s. So the vortex is still below the record low for the date.
- At 50 hPa the ECMWF ENS mean is 8.8 m/s, below the NASA record low of 10.1 m/s for 14 November.
- The 10 hPa polar cap is -58.8 °C in ECMWF HRES, still warmer than the NASA 90th percentile of -61.9 °C. It cools, so no new warming is under way.

No new reversal in the forecast:
- ECMWF ENS and AIFS ENS (machine learning, to 28 November), GEFS and GEPS (to 30 November) give 0% of members easterly on any day. Severe-weather.eu shows the same for 132 members.
- Weatheriscool gives 100% for ECMWF ENS, but that count includes the analysis days of 11-12 November.
- The lowest members are 3.6 m/s (ECMWF ENS), 3.0 m/s (AIFS ENS), 2.9 m/s (GEFS) and 2.7 m/s (GEPS), all on 14 November.
- Severe-weather.eu says no SSW is expected in two weeks. That is about a new event, and a reversal already happened.

Recovery:
- Means on 28 November: ECMWF ENS 26.1 m/s, GEPS 28.2 m/s, GEFS 36.3 m/s and AIFS ENS 33.2 m/s. The AIFS ENS bias at 12-16 days is +2.7 m/s, so about 30.5 m/s. The NASA mean for that date is 29.8 m/s.
- The 10 hPa polar cap cools to about -67 to -69 °C on 22-28 November, near the NASA mean.
- The ECMWF 46-day chart (13 November) has a mean of about 33 m/s on 4 December and about 40 m/s on 18-20 December. That is above its model climate of 33-35 m/s. On the chart, 1-2 members fall to about 0 m/s near 27-28 December. That is a value from the chart, not a numeric share.

Early-warning signs:
- The October pulse was large: 46.4 K m/s on 29 October in the ECMWF analysis (60°N). It was first wave 2 (27.1 K m/s on 28 October), then wave 1 (21.4 K m/s on 4 November).
- The NASA 45-day mean (45-75°N) is 12.4 K m/s, a record high for the date. Today the daily flux is low, 6.3 K m/s (severe-weather.eu, 45-75°N) against a mean of 13.0 K m/s.
- A second pulse comes on 21-23 November (60°N): AIFS 32.1 K m/s and GFS 27.1 K m/s on 21 November, ECMWF HRES 31.0 K m/s on 23 November (wave 2 16.8 K m/s). The ensemble means (45-75°N) peak near 20-21 K m/s, under their 90th percentile of 26.2 K m/s. The single-run peaks were not compared with a percentile.

Shape: a displacement now, then a stretch, not a split.
- Wave 1 at 10 hPa is 767 m, at the 96th percentile of this season's 25 days. Wave 2 is 124 m, at the 16th percentile.
- The ECMWF, GFS and ECMWF ENS mean 10 hPa maps agree on one vortex. It is pushed off the pole towards the Barents Sea and Siberia, with a high over Alaska.
- On 24 November the ECMWF ENS mean stretches it from Siberia towards Canada. By 29-30 November it sits near the pole in ECMWF ENS and GFS.
- AIFS (machine learning) agrees. Its cold pool lies over Scandinavia on 19 November and near Greenland at -76 to -80 °C on 24-29 November.
- Wave 2 grows to 488 m (HRES), 464 m (AIFS) and 375 m (GEM) on 23-24 November. Its ridges shift west with height, by -49° to -67° in HRES on 20-24 November. That is the structure of a split, but the wind rises to 20-25 m/s at the same time, so I read a stretch.

Depth: the two measures disagree.
- The 50 hPa wind stays westerly in every member. The ECMWF ENS mean is 7.9 m/s on 23 November, near the NASA 10th percentile of 8.5 m/s. The weakest member is 4.2 m/s on 27 November.
- The 100 hPa polar cap reached +2.19 sd in the HRES analysis on 4 November. Today it is +0.52 to +0.63 sd.
- Members at +1 sd at 100 hPa on any day: GEPS 81%, AIFS ENS 63%, ECMWF ENS 61% and GEFS 6%. Daily peaks are 47% (ECMWF ENS, 23-25 November), 57% (AIFS ENS) and 67% (GEPS), both on 24 November.
- So the event is deep by the cap rule, although the 50 hPa wind stays westerly.
- At 500 hPa, ECMWF ENS has 27% of members at +1 sd on 23 November, 49% on 24 November and 55-59% on 25-27 November. The first day with half the members is 25 November, and 75% get there on some day.
- Single runs at 500 hPa: HRES +1.84 sd on 28 November, GEM +1.04 sd on 24 November, GFS +0.49 sd, AIFS +0.45 sd and UKMO -0.15 sd.

models.view: Analysis -2.0 m/s on 11-12 November. stratosphere.winter_impact:
The major SSW of 10-12 November is in the analysis. A new one cannot start before about 3 December, 20 westerly days after the last easterly day. No ensemble member reverses again to 28-30 November. After an SSW, another one started within 60 days in 2 of 31 cases since 1979, and in 0 of 4 early cases.

The surface window starts when the 500 hPa polar cap turns positive in the ensembles. ECMWF ENS first has half of its members at +1 sd on 25 November. So the window opens on about 24-28 November.

From about 7 December the vortex rebuilds to about 38-40 m/s in the ECMWF 46-day run. A strong vortex favours mild, wet westerlies, so the cold risk falls in the second half of December.
