winter_outlook.summary:
My call is a near-normal winter with a mild lean, and my confidence is low. The best cold chances are a cold week to 23 November and a block from late November to mid-December. February holds a second, smaller easterly risk.

The odds are:
- December to February colder than the 1991-2020 normal: 30% (medium).
- A cold spell of 5 days or more from 1 November to 31 March: 48% (medium).
- December to February wetter than the mean of 209 mm: 47%.
- More stormy days than the mean of 17.6: 44%.
- A major sudden stratospheric warming that starts in November: 99%. December 3%, January 18%, February 22%.

A major sudden stratospheric warming started on 10 November, and it reaches down. More than half of the ECMWF members take the 500 hPa polar cap to +1 sd on 25 to 27 November. But the models put the high over Scandinavia and the low west of Ireland. That gives Edinburgh a south-easterly from a continent that is not cold, so temperatures stay near normal. The vortex then rebuilds fast, to about 38 m/s by mid-December.

The background points mild. A very strong El Nino, a westerly QBO, a warm North Sea and little snow upwind all work against cold that lasts. Seven of eight seasonal centres show a strongly negative NAO in February, with the low near the UK. That keeps a late easterly risk open.
winter_outlook.basis:
I start from the 1991-2020 base rates, because the normals come from that period. At Edinburgh, cold December to February is 40%, a cold spell 43%, a wet winter 37% and a stormy winter 50%. The last 15 winters give 27%, 40%, 47% and 47%. The record warms by 0.24 degC a decade, so a December to February colder than the fixed line is less common now. I begin the drivers from about 31% for cold, 42% for a spell, 41% for wet and 48% for stormy.

The season data run to 8 November, with no spell days and no stormy days yet. My calls score only when the winter ends, so I have no bias to correct. My 12 calls so far average 28% for cold and 45% for a spell.

A major sudden stratospheric warming started on 10 November. NASA GEOS had -2.9 m/s at 60N and 10 hPa on 11 November and -2.1 m/s on 12 November, record lows for the dates. All ECMWF ENS and AIFS ENS members were easterly on 11 and 12 November. The wind is westerly again at 3 to 4 m/s on 14 November, still below the ERA5 lowest for the date of 9.2 m/s. This is the earliest major warming in the NASA MERRA-2 record since 1979/80, which started in December 1981 before.

The upper vortex recovers fast. The ECMWF ENS mean is 24.3 m/s on 24 November, near the NASA 30th percentile, and 26.1 m/s on 28 November. GEFS is faster, at 36.3 m/s on 28 November, near the 60th percentile. No member of ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS, GEFS or GEPS reverses again to 28 to 30 November. The EC46 chart takes the mean to about 38 m/s near mid-December, a little above its model climate of about 34 m/s.

The two depth measures disagree, so I give both. The 50 hPa wind stays westerly at 7 to 12 m/s to late November, near the NASA 10th percentile. The 100 hPa polar cap reached +2.19 sd in the ECMWF analysis on 4 November. It returns above +1 sd on some day in 61% of ECMWF ENS members, 63% of AIFS ENS, 81% of GEPS and 13% of GEFS. Three of four ensembles show a clear share, so I call the event deep.

The 500 hPa cap sets the start of the surface window. ECMWF ENS takes 49% of members to +1 sd on 24 November and 59% on 26 November, with half from 25 November. The ensemble-mean cap peaks at +1.15 sd on 25 November, and 75% of members reach +1 sd on some day. The GFS single run reaches +0.49 sd at 500 hPa on 24 November, weaker and slower. Extended-range skill for the surface answer is modest, so I read the shares, not one run.

A negative AO is not the same as cold in Edinburgh. The ECMWF weekly maps for 23 to 30 November put +10 to +20 hPa over Scandinavia and a low west of Ireland. That gives a south-easterly from a continent that is not cold, and the UK runs 0 to +1 degC. The Edinburgh meteogram has that week near +0.5 degC and the December weeks at 0 to +0.5 degC. So the surface answer blocks the Atlantic, but it does not bring deep cold here.

The week before is colder. The meteogram has 16 to 23 November at about -2.7 degC, with every member below its model climate. The Hovmoller shows a trough near 0 to 25E on about 16 to 19 November. Then it shows a ridge over the UK on 20 to 24 November. It shows no clear trough over eastern Europe with a ridge to the west to 15 December, so no long northerly window. The regime schemes disagree on 17 to 20 November, so I trust the meteogram temperatures, not the labels.

The ECMWF ENS mean 10 hPa maps put the vortex off the pole towards Scandinavia on 19 November. It stretches from Canada to Siberia on 24 November and returns to the pole on 29 November. From 20 November the wave-2 ridges near the Urals and Alaska tilt west with height, by -49 to -67 degrees in ECMWF HRES. The 10 hPa wind rises at the same time, so I read a stretch, not a split. The hebweather centroid moves from 67 to 70N back to 80 to 85N by day 15.

The first wave pulse peaked at 46.4 K m/s on 29 October, the size of the run-up to the March 2026 event. A second pulse comes on 21 to 23 November in several runs. ECMWF HRES has 29.2 to 31.0 K m/s, mostly wave 2, and GFS and AIFS reach 27.1 and 32.1 K m/s. It meets a vortex that rebuilds, so it stretches the vortex but reverses it in no member.

A cold surge pressed a high against the Tibetan Plateau on 8 and 9 November, with a mountain torque over East Asia of +4.0 sd. Global angular momentum rose from +0.3 sd on 7 November to +2.91 sd on 14 November. The Global Wind Oscillation is in phase 6 at 3.08, the El Nino state with an extended Pacific jet. The chain follows in part: the PNA is +1.6, and GEFS has 48% of members at an EPO of -1 or below on 21 November. ECMWF ENS has only 35% on 25 November. The wave pulse on 21 to 23 November is the next link.

El Nino is very strong and east Pacific. The ONI is +2.46, the RONI +1.97 and the MEI v2 +2.53, rank 1 of 48. Nino 1+2 at +5.6 degC and Nino 3 at +4.4 degC are records, with E at +4.71 against C at +1.63. By flavour the nearest same weeks are 1997, and by Nino 3.4 they are 2015. The week of relative Nino 3.4 is +1.87 degC, and the PNA of +1.6 shows that the atmosphere follows the ocean.

The class tables are one reference class in an older climate. On the RONI, Edinburgh had cold December to February in 2 of 5 very strong winters, within chance. Since 1990, the 4 winters at +1.0 or more were all milder, at +0.80 degC, milder than chance. Central England's 7 very strong winters averaged +1.20 degC against their era, with none colder. Each table holds about as many results outside chance as chance gives, so I take a mild tilt, not a rule.

The seasonal maps are the November issue, with a start of 1 November, so they do not include the warming that began on 10 November. C3S, SEAS5 and GloSea put the UK at 0 to +1 degC for the whole winter. But the SEAS5 NAO medians are about -1.5 in January and -2.9 in February. Seven of the eight centres and the multi-system mean show a strongly negative NAO in February. Most of them have the low over the UK or western Europe. Seasonal models understate the NAO, so I weight this February signal up. On balance they move the December to February cold odds up by about 2 points. The mild temperature maps pull down, and the strong February NAO signal pulls back.

This NAO signal disagrees with the fast vortex rebuild for January, so I keep January mild and hold the cold tilt for February. The SEAS5 point numbers lean mild. The raw share colder than normal is 39%, but it mixes EC46 for December with the SEAS5 cold bias of -0.67 degC. SEAS5 alone against its own climate gives 24%, or 20% to 27% after we round the values. The same SEAS5 members against the ERA5 normal give 53%. EC46 now makes December 4.6 degC against 4.1 degC, with 71% of members warmer.

The QBO is westerly, +15.9 m/s at 30 hPa and +13.5 m/s at 50 hPa in October. It favours a fast rebuild and fewer mid-winter disruptions. The MJO is weak, phase 4 at 1.08 on 10 November. ECMWF ENS takes it to phase 4 near 1.5 at day 5, then back inside the circle. GEFS keeps it near or inside the circle in phases 3 and 4 to 28 November. So neither reaches phases 6 and 7.

The North Sea is +0.77 degC against 1991-2020, with 36% of cells above +1 degC. It is a little cooler than my last outlook, which had +0.98 degC. It still gives heavy showers in an easterly but keeps snow at the coast marginal. The tripole is -0.61, a weak positive-NAO pattern. The Barents and Kara Seas are +1.73 degC in open water, linked to a weaker vortex. Eurasian snow is 14.55 million km2, below the normal of 16.06 and rank 41 of 61.

Upwind, Oslo has snow on the ground in 55% to 76% of members after 16 November, but Stockholm and Helsinki have almost none. Cold air aloft builds to the north-east late in the month. On 26 November, 39% of members reach -8 degC at 850 hPa over Helsinki and 31% over Oslo. Copenhagen, the nearest point on the easterly track, reaches it in only 12%.

The ECMWF regimes of 13 November make Scandinavian blocking the most likely on 22 to 27 November and 7 to 12 December. NAO+ is the most likely on 2 and 3 December and 13 to 21 December. Simon Lee's index of 12 November agrees on the block near 22 November. After that it keeps NAO- near +0.8 sd to 20 December, so the two schemes differ in December. EC46 of 14 November has Arctic pressure at +0.64 sd and +0.59 sd in the weeks from 23 and 30 November. It falls near 0 from 14 December.

The EC46 NAO mean is -0.35 sd in the week from 30 November, with 22% of members at -1 or below. Against ECMWF's re-forecast climate, the NAO stays 5.5 to 7.9 hPa below normal in every December week. The two baselines differ in size, but both lean negative. Skill past week 3 is modest, so I read the shares, not a date.

Judah Cohen's blog of 9 November expects a stretched vortex, cold in East Asia and North America, and a short positive AO. I agree on the stretch and on the positive AO, which GEFS has at +0.5 to +1.0 on 16 to 22 November. I differ on two points. The 10 hPa wind reversed, so this is a major warming under the scored rule. And ECMWF ENS takes the 500 hPa cap to +1 sd in 59% of members, so the troposphere answers.

The Met Office text for 19 to 28 November has a cold north with frost and wintry showers on high ground, and I agree. For 29 November to 13 December it has a high between Scandinavia and Greenland and a colder north. I agree on the block. But the ECMWF maps keep the UK at 0 to +1 degC with the low to the west. So I give snow and ice in early December less weight than the text does.

The analog set is outside the record, with no measurable skill, so I give it no weight. The nearest winters on El Nino and the QBO alone are 2015/16, 1997/98, 1982/83, 1987/88 and 2002/03. They average +0.2 degC, within chance. The 4 winters with a major warming by 31 December averaged -0.3 degC, also within chance. No winter in the record had a November warming, so the record has no precedent. In Central England, May to October 2026 was near the warmest on record. A cold November there leads to a cold winter 38% of the time, against 33% for all winters.

So I set cold December to February at 30%, a medium chance. The deep warming, the block to mid-December and the February NAO signal lift it. El Nino, the westerly QBO, the strong rebuild in mid-December and the mild EC46 December hold it down. I put it above the SEAS5 own-climate 24%, because that issue predates the warming. I put it below the raw 39%, because that share carries the model cold bias.

I set the cold spell at 48%, medium. The week to 23 November is cold, but a showery north-westerly seldom gives 5 nights at -3 degC in a row. The block from late November and the February easterly risk give later chances. The very strong El Nino class had a spell in 3 of 5 winters, within chance.

I set the wet winter at 47%. The seasonal low over the UK, the warm North Sea and the warm western Atlantic lift it from the base. The SEAS5 point data give about 109% of normal, and C3S gives 100% to 110%.

I set the stormy winter at 44%. A negative NAO moves the jet south, and the cold winters of 2012/13, 2017/18 and 2020/21 had only 6 to 14 stormy days. These are not mirrors of the cold odds, because a winter can be wet, stormy and cold at once.

For the warming months, November is 99%, because the event started on 10 November and the wind recovers well. December is 3%. A new event cannot start before about 3 December, after 20 westerly days. No member of the shorter ensembles reverses to 30 November. On the EC46 chart, one or two members touch 0 m/s near 27 to 28 December, about 1% to 2%.

January is 18%, below the 22% reference. The El Nino model gives 27%, from 25% to 29%, but its hindcast does no better than the reference. The westerly QBO and the record after early warmings, 0 of 4 followed within 60 days, pull it down. February is 22%, at the reference, because the El Nino tilt and the westerly QBO cancel. The class cell for this winter, 0 of 3, is too few winters to tell. Other people's dated calls do not move my numbers.

My last outlook gave 30% cold, 48% for a spell, 47% wet and 44% stormy, and warming odds of 99%, 3%, 18% and 22%. This run uses the same ECMWF run of 13 November and the same GEFS of 14 November. Thus the evidence is the same and my odds do not change. I go through the last would_change signs below.

Its colder signs stand as follows:
- ECMWF members at +1 sd at 500 hPa on 25 to 30 November reach 50%: this still holds, at 55% to 59% on 25 to 27 November, but the observed AO is -0.87 on 14 November and not yet below -1.
- Scandinavian blocking or NAO- most likely on most days of 1 to 15 December with the low south of Scotland: not met. There is a block on 7 to 12 December, with the low to the west.
- 30% of members at -8 degC over Copenhagen on 1 to 10 December: we cannot judge this yet, because the data end on 28 November. So far, at most 12% reach it.
- A 100 hPa heat flux above 25 K m/s on 3 days of 19 to 26 November: a forecast pulse of 27 to 31 K m/s on 21 to 23 November, not yet in the analysis.
- EC46 members easterly at 10 hPa in late December or January: not met, with one or two members near 0 m/s in late December.
- The SEAS5 and C3S December issues: not out yet, near 5 December.

Its milder signs stand as follows:
- Most members below +1 sd at 500 hPa on 25 to 30 November: this went the other way, with 59% at +1 sd.
- NAO+ most likely on most days of 1 to 15 December: not met, with NAO+ on 2 to 3 December and 13 to 21 December.
- The 10 hPa wind above 45 m/s by 15 December with a cold pole: not met, near 38 m/s, but the pole is cold.
- Every December week above +0.5 degC in Edinburgh: not clearly met, with the weeks at 0 to +0.5 degC.
- The SEAS5 December issue drops the NAO signal: not out yet.
No sign can no longer happen. The odds stay the same because the weather did not move since the last run, not because I give the same evidence a different weight.
cold_windows: 16-23 November (high): a cold north-westerly to northerly behind a trough near the North Sea. The ECMWF meteogram has the week at about -2.7 degC, with every member below its model climate. The city gets showers of rain, hail and sleet, with frost on clear nights. Five nights at -3 degC in a row are unlikely in a showery wind. The Pentlands get snow showers and a thin cover on the tops.

22 November to 12 December (medium): a blocking high over Scandinavia, first with a low west of Ireland. ECMWF makes Scandinavian blocking the most likely regime on 22 to 27 November and 7 to 12 December. The wind is south-easterly from a mild continent at first, so the city stays near normal, with fog, frost and cold rain on fronts. The Pentlands and Moorfoots get battleground snow if fronts stall against the block. A true easterly with snow showers needs the low south of Scotland and -8 degC air over Denmark. Only 12% of members show this on 26 November.

February (low): an easterly on the north side of a low over the UK and western Europe. Seven of eight seasonal centres show a strong Arctic high, and the SEAS5 NAO median is about -2.9. But SEAS5 alone keeps 65% of members warmer than its own February climate. The North Sea is +0.77 degC, so the air aloft must reach -8 degC for snow at the coast. The city gets snow that lies a day or two at best, and the Pentlands get lying snow for days.

17-31 December (low): a ridge near the UK with a trough over Scandinavia, or a second disruption of the vortex. The EC46 500 hPa map for 21 to 28 December has this shape, but NAO+ is the most likely regime on 13 to 21 December. One or two EC46 members reach 0 m/s at 10 hPa near 27 to 28 December. The city gets frost under the ridge and cold showers if the wind turns north. The hills get snow showers.

March (low): late frost and short snowfalls in northerly or easterly outbreaks. The SEAS5 NAO median is about -2.4, and the point data give 8 frost days against 5.7. The city gets frost and brief snow, and the hills get lying snow after each outbreak.

January (low): mostly westerly or north-westerly flow behind a vortex that EC46 rebuilds to about 38 m/s in late December. Four centres put a low near the UK, wet and near normal, and NCEP and Meteo-France put it over Scandinavia. The city gets rain, sleet in showers and frost on clear nights. Snow to low levels needs a block, and the warming chance is 18%.

snow_checklist: ✅ Polar vortex weakens or breaks down: the 60N wind at 10 hPa reversed on 10 to 12 November, with -2.9 m/s on 11 November in NASA GEOS. This is the earliest reversal in the record. It is westerly again at 3 to 4 m/s on 14 November and rebuilds to 24 to 36 m/s by 28 November.

🟡 AO and NAO negative for 2 weeks or more: both were negative from 9 November. The AO was -1.98 on 12 November and -0.87 on 14 November. GEFS turns the AO positive on 16 to 22 November, then back to -1.48 by 29 November with 90% of members negative.

🟡 Blocking high over Scandinavia or Greenland: no block sits there in the analysis. ECMWF makes Scandinavian blocking the most likely regime on 22 to 27 November, with +10 to +20 hPa over Scandinavia in the week from 23 November.

🟡 Cold air in place upwind: Oslo has snow, but Stockholm and Helsinki have almost none, and Eurasian snow ranks 41 of 61. At 850 hPa, 39% of members reach -8 degC over Helsinki and 31% over Oslo on 26 November.

⬜ Cold enough aloft, about -8 degC at 850 hPa: Copenhagen is the nearest point on the easterly track. It reaches -8 degC in at most 12% of members to 28 November. The North Sea is +0.77 degC, so coast snow needs colder air than usual.
⬜ It happens more than once, or lasts: no spell meets the rule yet, with 0 days to 8 November. The chances are the cold week to 23 November and the block from late November.
⬜ El Nino's grip loosens: the ONI is +2.46, the MEI v2 +2.53, a record, and the PNA +1.6. SEAS5 keeps Nino 3.4 near +4.0 degC in December and January and near +3.7 degC in February.

months.notes: The warming started on 10 November, and the AO fell to -1.98 on 12 November. The meteogram has 16 to 23 November at about -2.7 degC, with every member below its model climate. A Scandinavian block follows from 22 November with the low to the west, near +0.5 degC. The snow risk is mostly on the Pentlands, with sleet showers in the city.

ECMWF regimes make Scandinavian blocking the most likely on 7 to 12 December and NAO+ on 13 to 21 December. The weekly maps keep the UK at 0 to +1 degC, with the low to the west or south-west. EC46 gives 4.6 degC against the 4.1 degC normal, with 71% of members warmer, and 86 mm against 77 mm. Fronts that stall against the block give battleground snow on the hills. The normal is 3.4 snow days, mostly sleet in the city.

Four centres and the multi-system mean put a low near the UK or western Europe under a Greenland high. NCEP and Meteo-France put the low over Scandinavia, a north-westerly. SEAS5 alone keeps 76% of members warmer than its own January climate. The point data give 4.0 degC against 3.9 degC and 74 mm against 74 mm. The warming chance is 18%, and the normal is 4.7 snow days.

Seven of eight centres show a strongly negative NAO, and the SEAS5 median is about -2.9. Most put the low over the UK or western Europe, so Scotland sits near its north edge, an easterly risk. But SEAS5 alone keeps 65% of members warmer than its own February climate. The point data give 3.8 degC against 4.1 degC and 69 mm against 62 mm. The warming chance is 22%, and the normal is 3.8 snow days.

The SEAS5 NAO median is about -2.4, and GloSea keeps an Arctic high with lower pressure over Europe. SEAS5 alone keeps 75% of members warmer than its own March climate. The point data give 5.0 degC against 5.3 degC, with 8 frost days against 5.7. A late block can bring frost and short snowfalls. The normal is 3.2 snow days.

drivers: Polar vortex: a major sudden stratospheric warming started on 10 November. NASA GEOS shows -2.9 m/s at 60N and 10 hPa on 11 November, a record low. The wind is 3 to 4 m/s on 14 November, below the ERA5 lowest for the date of 9.2 m/s. It is the earliest warming in the NASA MERRA-2 record since 1979/80.

Depth: the two measures disagree. The 50 hPa wind stays westerly at 7 to 12 m/s, near the 10th percentile. The 100 hPa cap reached +2.19 sd on 4 November. It returns above +1 sd in 61% of ECMWF ENS, 63% of AIFS ENS, 81% of GEPS and 13% of GEFS members. So the event is deep.

Surface answer: ECMWF ENS takes the 500 hPa cap to +1 sd in half of its members from 25 November, 59% on 26 November. But the low sits west of Ireland and the high over Scandinavia. So Edinburgh gets a south-easterly near normal, not deep cold.

Shape: the ECMWF ENS mean puts the vortex off the pole towards Scandinavia on 19 November. On 24 November, it stretches the vortex from Canada to Siberia. It is back on the pole on 29 November. Wave-2 ridges near the Urals and Alaska tilt west with height, but the wind rises, so this is a stretch, not a split.

Wave forcing: the 100 hPa heat flux peaked at 46.4 K m/s on 29 October. A second pulse of 27 to 32 K m/s comes on 21 to 23 November, mostly wave 2. It meets a vortex that rebuilds, so it reverses the vortex in no member.

Pacific chain: the mountain torque over East Asia reached +4.0 sd on 8 November, and angular momentum rose from +0.3 sd to +2.91 sd by 14 November. The PNA is +1.6, and GEFS has 48% of members at an EPO of -1 or below on 21 November, ECMWF ENS only 35%. The chain follows in part.

El Nino: very strong and east Pacific, with the ONI at +2.46, the RONI at +1.97 and a record MEI v2 of +2.53. The nearest same weeks are 1997 by flavour and 2015 by Nino 3.4. The class leans mild here and in Central England, mostly within chance.
QBO: westerly, +15.9 m/s at 30 hPa and +13.5 m/s at 50 hPa in October. It favours a fast rebuild and fewer mid-winter disruptions, so it lowers the cold odds.
MJO: weak, phase 4 at 1.08 on 10 November. ECMWF ENS and GEFS keep it near phases 3 and 4 and mostly inside the circle, so neither gives a push to a negative NAO.

Angular momentum: +2.91 sd on 14 November, with the Global Wind Oscillation in phase 6 at 3.08, the El Nino state with an extended Pacific jet. A later move to phases 7 and 8 favours ridges, but it does not show yet.

Sea temperatures: the North Sea is +0.77 degC, cooler than my last outlook, so coast snow stays marginal. The tripole is -0.61, a weak positive-NAO sign. The Barents and Kara Seas are +1.73 degC, linked to a weaker vortex.

Snow and cold upwind: Eurasian snow is 14.55 million km2, rank 41 of 61, below the normal of 16.06. Oslo has snow, Stockholm and Helsinki do not, and Copenhagen reaches -8 degC at 850 hPa in at most 12% of members.

Extended range: ECMWF regimes give Scandinavian blocking on 22 to 27 November and 7 to 12 December, and NAO+ on 13 to 21 December. EC46 keeps Arctic pressure near +0.6 sd to early December, then near 0.

Seasonal models: the November issue predates the warming. It puts the UK at 0 to +1 degC, but seven of eight centres show a strongly negative NAO in February. I weight the NAO signal up and the mild maps down.
Analogs: outside the record, with no measurable skill, so they get no weight. The nearest El Nino and QBO winters average +0.2 degC, and the 4 early-warming winters -0.3 degC, both within chance.

'Claude (this page)' is your own previous forecasts, scored the same way (its rain call counts a chance of 50% or more, or medium or high risk, as rain); use its biases to correct yourself. items.title: ECMWF seasonal ensemble by month for Edinburgh vs ERA5 1991-2020 normals. This is Open-Meteo's default seasonal series: EC46 (run daily) for about the first 46 days, then SEAS5 (started on the 1st of each month), 51 members joined by member number, on a 36 km grid, so the first month or two are mostly EC46. Raw model output, not bias-corrected: the model's own climate at this point differs from ERA5's normal by month and lead (the SEAS5 winter call's model_climate.by_month gives bias_c, and pct_members_warmer_than_model_climate for SEAS5 alone against its own climate), so pct_members_warmer_than_normal here mixes the forecast with that bias. Compare the spread and the shares, not the absolute values

ECMWF's own implied calls on the cold-winter event, from the point members. pct_members_colder_than_normal (logged beside your call and scored as the rival 'ECMWF SEAS5') is the share of the 51 members of the default series above (EC46 for about 46 days, then SEAS5, joined by member number, so its December is mostly EC46) with a December-February mean of (daily max + min) / 2 below the ERA5 1991-2020 normal. It is raw model output, so it mixes the forecast with the model's own error at this point, and it is against ERA5, not the ERA5-Land the odds are scored on. pct_members_colder_than_model_climate is SEAS5 alone (model_climate.run_start is the first month of the reply; in the first days of a month the newest run can still be the month before): the share of its members whose December-February mean is below SEAS5's own climate for the same start month and lead (ECMWF's monthly anomaly, from its re-forecasts; model_climate.climate says which years). That removes the model's mean error at this point (model_climate.by_month gives it month by month as bias_c, the model climate minus the ERA5 normal) but not errors in the spread, and it is not calibrated on the model's past skill. model_climate.djf.pct_range_for_rounding is how far the 0.1 °C rounding of ECMWF's figures can move it; pct_same_members_colder_than_era5_normal is the same SEAS5 members against the ERA5 normal without the correction, so the three shares separate the EC46 part from the bias part. None of them is the answer: they are inputs to weigh

items.title: Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later; w1 and w2 are the parts of it carried by zonal wavenumbers 1 and 2: a pulse mostly in wave 1 tends to displace the vortex, one with a large wave-2 part to stretch and split it), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-11-14 are analysis.

items.title: East Pacific Oscillation, computed by this page: the cos(latitude)-weighted mean 500 hPa height anomaly over 20-35°N, 160-125°W minus that over 55-65°N, 160-125°W, divided by the sd of the difference for the day of year (NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1, 1991-2020, trend carried forward). Negative = a ridge over Alaska: Arctic air into North America, and often more upward wave flux into the stratosphere a week or two later, so read it beside the 100 hPa heat flux. Positive = a trough near Alaska and mild Pacific air. Ensembles give the mean, the 5th/25th/75th/95th percentiles and the share of members at -1 or below each day; single runs start 5 days back. Days before 2026-11-14 are analysis. It can differ a little from other sites' EPO, which use other climatologies and grids

periods.text: A changeable pattern is likely to continue, with areas of rain or showers affecting parts of the UK, particularly across the south and west. These will be interspersed with drier, colder interludes as shorter-lived ridges of high pressure develop. Weather patterns may become slower evolving during the latter stages of November, leading to some uncertainty over how much progress Atlantic frontal systems will make into the UK. Nonetheless, further rain or showers are likely at times, with the potential for some periods of strong winds. Incursions of milder air are likely towards the south, although it could remain on the cold side overall further north, where there is potential for overnight frosts and occasional wintry precipitation, particularly over higher ground.

The tracks of low pressure may shift farther south over the North Atlantic into December, as high pressure potentially builds between Scandinavia and Greenland. Whilst there remains some uncertainty over which of these features will have the greater influence on the weather in the UK, some rain is likely at times, particularly across southern areas, whilst northern and especially northwestern parts may become drier than normal. Milder incursions are possible in the south, although this pattern would also bring an increased chance of colder conditions developing, particularly in the north, along with associated winter hazards such as snow and ice.
